text: Garneray went to sea at thirteen, encouraged by a cousin who commanded the frigate Forte. He served as a corsair under Robert Surcouf and Jean-Marie Dutertre. The British then held him as a prisoner of war aboard prison hulks for eight years. He was the eldest son of Jean-François Garneray, a painter of the king who had studied under Jacques-Louis David. After the Napoleonic Wars ended he went on painting until he died in 1857. He wrote too.

Skredsvig grew up on the Skredsvig farm in Modum. At fifteen he began at Johan Fredrik Eckersberg's painting school in Christiania. He then spent four years in Copenhagen under the landscape painter Vilhelm Kyhn. In 1875 he settled in Munich, where he made lifelong friends among the Norwegian artists living there, and next he moved to Paris, where he studied for a time under Léon Bonnat. He was a writer too.

Elizabeth Thompson painted battles. She specialised in scenes from British campaigns, among them the Crimean War and the Napoleonic Wars. Queen Victoria bought The Roll Call, and she also painted The Defence of Rorke's Drift and Scotland Forever!, which shows the Scots Greys at Waterloo. Her sister was the essayist and poet Alice Meynell. After she married the army officer William Butler she was known as Lady Butler. She wrote in 1922 that she never painted for the glory of war, but to portray its pathos and heroism.

Fernando Yáñez de la Almedina came from Almedina in Spain and may have been of morisco origin. He went to Italy to study and there got to know the work of Leonardo da Vinci. After he came back to Spain he worked with Hernando de los Llanos on many pictures. His Saint Catherine of Alexandria is in the Prado. The Metropolitan Museum owns his Head of Christ from 1506. He died after 1537.

George van der Mijn came from a family of painters in Amsterdam. His father Herman was born in London, after the grandfather moved there. Johan van Gool wrote about the family, including George's brothers Robert, Francis, Andreas and Gerard and his sister Cornelia, who all painted. Another brother, Willem, might have been a good painter too, but he fell through the ice while skating and died young. George made portraits and genre works, and his pupil was Dirk van Dijl.

Guillaumet failed to win the Prix de Rome for historical landscape in 1861, so he crossed the Mediterranean to Algeria instead. He caught malaria there and spent three months in the military hospital in Biskra. Still, he went back to Algeria ten times by 1867. He preferred to travel in the south, and many of his works show the life of desert people. Before that he had studied under François-Edouard Picot and Félix-Joseph Barrias. He was born in Puteaux, near Paris.

Jacob Munch served as a military officer. He studied at the academy in Copenhagen and later in Paris, where Jacques-Louis David was his teacher. Afterwards he worked in Italy and Germany, painting portraits of famous people. Christian Frederik, the future Danish king, invited him to Norway in 1813. His biggest assignment was a picture of the coronation of Charles XIV John at Nidaros Cathedral. In 1818 he co-founded the Norwegian National Academy of Craft and Art Industry and taught there.

Francesco Curia worked mostly in Naples. His father, Michele Curia, was a painter, and Francesco studied with Giovanni Filippo Criscuolo. Fabrizio Santafede and Ippolito Borghese were among his own pupils. Like several other artists in Naples, he was influenced by the style of Giorgio Vasari. He lived from about 1538 until 1610, and Naples is where he spent his working life.

Nicolas Pineau carved and designed ornament, and he was one of the men who started the rocaille, or Rococo, style in France. His father Jean-Baptiste was a carver too. In 1716 he went to St. Petersburg with Alexandre Le Blond, among the designers and craftsmen in that group. When Le Blond died in 1719, Pineau became the leading French decorative artist in Russia. His chief work there was the Grand Cabinet of Peter the Great at Peterhof, which the Tsar showed off, newly complete, in August 1721. He also worked in Paris.

Gifford grew up near New Bedford, though he came from Nonamesset Island in the Elizabeth Islands. As a teenager he painted ships together with the Dutch painter Albertus Van Beest. He leaned toward the Barbizon school. He opened a studio in Boston in 1864 and moved to New York City two years later. He became a full member of the National Academy of Design in 1878. He painted in Oregon and California, then traveled in Europe, Morocco and Egypt, where artists such as Louis Comfort Tiffany joined him.

Koller grew up in Zurich at the Schwarzen Adler hotel, run by his father, a butcher and brewer turned innkeeper. The guests were mostly waggoners and cattle dealers, so he saw horses and cattle every day. His first art lessons came from an uncle who painted landscapes, and he decided early to specialise in horses. He shared a Paris studio with Böcklin. At the Louvre he copied Netherlandish art of the 17th century. Cows in Swiss landscapes later earned him the label painter of the Swiss national animal.

William Haskell Coffin painted women for magazine covers, among them The Saturday Evening Post, Redbook and McCall's. He grew up in Washington, DC, where he went to the Corcoran School of Art. After a short time back in his native Charleston painting portraits of society ladies, he went to France in 1902 to finish his training. He was one of the most highly paid illustrators of his day. The US government also commissioned posters from him.

Zanobi Strozzi worked in Florence and nearby Fiesole as a painter and manuscript illuminator. Vasari says he was a pupil of Fra Angelico, and most of Strozzi's surviving works are illuminations. He is also the painter once known as the Master of the Buckingham Palace Madonna. Vasari adds that he painted pictures and panels for many private houses in Florence. Strozzi may have been a pioneer of small narrative pictures for the home, which departed from the usual Virgin and Child. Vasari also mentions a double portrait by him.

Alexandre Falguière trained at the École des Beaux-Arts and won the Prix de Rome in 1859. His first important bronze, The Victor of the Cockfight, was shown in the Luxembourg Museum and is now in the Musée d'Orsay, along with Tarcisius the Christian Boy-Martyr. He also made monuments to Admiral Courbet and to Joan of Arc. The Dancer, a sculpture based on Cléo de Mérode, is in the Orsay too. He worked as a painter as well as a sculptor.

Dunouy's paintings were mostly small and decorative, and he is counted among the artists called little masters. A native of Paris, he began with views of the city and its surroundings and first showed at the Salon in 1791. He traveled to Italy in 1810 under the patronage of Joachim Murat. Jean-Louis Demarne and Nicolas Antoine Taunay added figures to some of his landscapes. He may have taught Achille-Etna Michallon.

Picot studied with François-André Vincent and Jacques-Louis David, and he won the Prix de Rome in 1813. His neoclassical Cupid and Psyche made his name at the Salon of 1819, and it hangs in the Louvre. He painted The Crowning of the Virgin for the church of Notre-Dame-de-Lorette. He also had large commissions for the Galerie des Batailles. He died in Paris in 1868.

Bisschop painted many of his interior scenes in Hindeloopen, a town known for keeping its traditional costume. He was the son of a prominent merchant in Leeuwarden. His teachers included Jacobus Schoemaker Doyer in Amsterdam and Huib van Hove at the academy in The Hague. Then came Paris and Charles Gleyre. In 1855 he opened a studio in The Hague, and he exhibited in the Netherlands, France and England. He also showed work at the Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia.

Jacobus Stellingwerff drew with a pen, and he made topographical sketches that were turned into prints. He drew in the style of Roelant Roghman. He was born and died in Amsterdam. He married Antonina Houbraken, who assisted him in his business. He often copied sketches that other artists had made from life, and those artists were sometimes not very accurate. Most of his work can be seen in the topographical atlas of Matheus Brouërius van Nidek.

André Le Nôtre grew up inside the Tuileries, because his father Jean was head gardener there. As a boy he studied mathematics, painting and architecture, and in the studio of Simon Vouet he met the painter Charles Le Brun. In 1637 he took over his father's job. Later he was put in charge of all the royal gardens of France. With Louis Le Vau and Le Brun he made the park at Vaux-le-Vicomte, and then he designed the gardens of Versailles.

Bolomey, a Swiss painter and politician, was the son of a Lausanne hotelier and trained in Paris as a pastel portrait painter. While there he became a pupil of Joseph-Marie Vien and was influenced by Boucher and La Tour. In 1763 he moved to The Hague and joined the Confrerie Pictura. He became court painter to William V, Prince of Orange, and painted Dutch society. From 1777 until 1791 he directed the Royal Academy of Art in The Hague, and then he returned to Lausanne.

Gherardo Cibo's great-grandfather was Pope Innocent VIII. Cibo grew up in a wealthy family in Genoa, and war kept him from joining the clergy. He studied botany in Bologna under Luca Ghini and began an herbarium in 1532, now the oldest surviving example of the Italian method. His plant drawings put the plant in the foreground and a landscape behind it. He spent most of his life in Arcevia. He also went by the name Ulisse Severini da Cingoli.

Heinrich Reinhold died at 36 after trying to talk his friend Johann Christoph Erhard out of suicide. He failed, and he fell terminally ill himself in the attempt. Reinhold is buried in the Protestant Cemetery in Rome, and his monument features sculpture by Bertel Thorvaldsen. He was born in Gera, the younger half-brother of the landscape painter Friedrich Philipp Reinhold. On the advice of Baron Denon he moved to Paris in 1809 and spent five years on a work about Napoleon's campaigns.

Rugendas came from the seventh generation of a family of painters and engravers in Augsburg. His great-grandfather, Georg Philipp Rugendas, was a celebrated painter of battles. In 1822 Rugendas reached Rio de Janeiro as the illustrator on Baron von Langsdorff's scientific expedition. He fell out with Langsdorff and left just before the expedition's journey to the Amazon. He stayed on in Brazil until 1825 and made mostly drawings and watercolors of daily life in Minas Gerais and Rio de Janeiro. He was influenced by Alexander von Humboldt.

Peszka's portrait of Hugo Kołłątaj brought him to the notice of members of the Great Sejm, and commissions for portraits of other political figures kept him busy until 1792. After that he made many trips through Lithuania and Russia, producing landscapes in watercolor and sepia. He spent time with his former mentor, Franciszek Smuglewicz, at Vilnius University. For a few years he served in Niasvizh as court painter to Prince Michał Hieronim Radziwiłł. In 1813 he returned to Kraków, where he had been born, and taught art.

Reinagle once sent a picture to the Royal Academy as his own work, though a young artist named Yarnold had painted it. He had bought it at a broker's shop and made slight changes. The academy investigated, and he had to resign his diploma. Before that he had trained with his father Philip Reinagle and exhibited at the academy as early as 1788. With Thomas Edward Barker he also ran a rival panorama in the Strand, with views of Rome, Florence, Gibraltar and Paris.

Antonio Molinari was nicknamed il Caraccino. He painted tumultuous narratives of mythology and religion on large canvases, and he was apprenticed to Antonio Zanchi in Venice. The vigorous, athletic paintings of Neapolitan artists such as Luca Giordano influenced him strongly. Many of his drawings survive, a large number of them in Düsseldorf. His preliminary studies in ink and chalk with wash show great speed in laying out a composition. Molinari has been called an artist of transition, but he was never a direct precursor of the Venetian styles of the 18th century.

Ida Gerhardi wanted to be a painter from childhood, but she was twenty-eight before she could start. Her father, a doctor, died in 1869, and the family moved to Detmold, where she grew up. In 1890 she enrolled at a women's academy and studied with the landscape painter Tina Blau. The next year she moved to Paris and studied at the Académie Colarossi, a popular school for foreign students. There she befriended the composer Frederick Delius. She spent much of her career in Paris as a Neo-Impressionist painter.

Jacques Chéreau published optical prints from a shop on the Rue Saint-Jacques in Paris. He also engraved portraits. He was the son of a carpenter in Blois. He worked for a year in England, where vue optique prints were made, and then with his older brother François, who had studied with Pierre Drevet and Gérard Audran. François bought Audran's plates in 1718. In 1722 Jacques married Anne Antoinette Yvart, the daughter of the painter Joseph Yvart.

Jan Collaert II worked in Antwerp as an engraver and also published under the name Jan Baptist Collaert. He trained with his brother Adriaen and with the Antwerp engravers Philip Galle and Gerard de Jode. He worked for Galle, one of the most prolific print publishers in Europe in the late sixteenth century. Both brothers married Galle's daughters. Jan joined the Guild of Saint Luke in 1585 and became its dean in 1612.

Jan van Dornicke came from Doornik, now also known as Tournai, and was active in Antwerp from about 1509 to about 1525. His paintings are classed as Antwerp Mannerism. He may be the same person as the Master of 1518. His first name is sometimes spelled Janssone, and his last name appears as van Doornik or van Dornick. He should not be confused with an eighteenth-century Dutch artist who had the same name.

Jean Leon Gerome Ferris was named after Jean-Léon Gérôme, the teacher his father admired. His father, Stephen James Ferris, was a portrait painter, and the painters Edward Moran and Thomas Moran were his uncles. He grew up around art. In 1879 he enrolled at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts. He is best known for The Pageant of a Nation, a series of 78 scenes from American history. It is the largest series of American historical paintings by a single artist.

Jean-Pierre Granger reportedly became a drum major at six, in the Régiment Royal-Bonbons, a children's branch of the French Guards. His father was a glazier. Two years later the father met the watercolorist Angélique Briceau, who gave both of them lessons. Granger worked as an engraver for seven years but felt constrained. Later he painted portraits, history paintings and mythological scenes in the Neo-Classical style. Some sources wrongly call him Jean-Perrin.

Passavant's catalogues of old master prints are still used, because some collections still follow his numbering. He moved to Paris in 1809 to look after business interests, and he returned to Frankfurt in 1824, when art history took over his attention. His Tour of a German Artist in England remains a significant source for art historians. In 1839 he became curator of the Städelsches Kunstinstitut in Frankfurt. There he acquired important prints and drawings, mounted exhibitions and taught. As a young man he had corresponded with the artist Franz Pforr.

James de Hamilton, a Scottish painter, taught his son Johann Georg to paint in Munich, where the boy was born. From 1689 Johann Georg worked as a court painter in Vienna. After that he moved to Berlin, but he was back in Vienna after 1718. He is known for hunting scenes. So is his brother Philipp Ferdinand. He is counted as an 18th-century painter from the Southern Netherlands who was active in Austria.

Jusepe Leonardo, also called José Leonardo, came from Calatayud and was a pupil of Eugenio Caxés. He became known for battle paintings. As painter to the king, he made works for the Buen Retiro palace, among them the Surrender of Juliers. A portrait of Alaric the Goth is in the Royal collections. He was one of the artists who decorated the Royal Alcazar of Madrid. With Félix Castello he also painted the vaults of the Sacristy of the Royal Chapel.

Leon Chwistek worked as a logician and as a painter. He mainly worked in the philosophy of science and mathematical logic, and he was one of the founders of the Polish Mathematical Society. As an artist he represented Polish Formism, which drew on Cubist and Futurist ideas. His father was a physician who opened one of the first hydrotherapy establishments in Zakopane. His mother was a pianist and a painter who had studied with Jan Matejko. Growing up in Zakopane, he became close friends with Stanisław Ignacy Witkiewicz.

Before he painted ships, Louis-Philippe Crépin sailed them, with four years as a helmsman. He studied marine painting with Joseph Vernet and landscapes with Hubert Robert. His first exhibit in Paris, in 1796, was La sortie du port de Brest. In 1817 the Minister of the Navy gave him a twenty-year commission for marine paintings, and he set up a workshop at the ministry. In 1830 he and Théodore Gudin became the first two Peintres de la Marine in France.

Nothing is known for certain about the Master of the Brunswick Diptych. He is named after a diptych in Brunswick that shows Mary with the infant Jesus and Saint Anne on one side, and a kneeling Carthusian monk with Saint Barbara on the other. Other paintings have been identified as by the same hand. Some scholars have suggested he was Jacob van Haarlem, but that is speculation. His work resembles that of Geertgen tot Sint Jans, though his colours are lighter and his treatment of space and anatomy is less accomplished.

Little is known about the life of Polidoro da Lanciano. He was born in Lanciano in the Abruzzi, and his grandfather Alessandro Rienzo painted ceramics there. His talent showed early, so he moved to Venice, the center of art in that region of Italy. There he took the Venetian form of his name, Lanzani. His birth year, 1515, is worked out from Venetian documents. He was first mentioned there in 1536.

Roubiliac took second place in the Prix de Rome competition in 1730, so he went to London instead of Rome. In 1738 his seated figure of Handel, made for Jonathan Tyers of Vauxhall Gardens, made him famous. Handel wears modern dress but plays an ancient Greek lyre, and a putto sits at his feet. The statue is now in the Victoria and Albert Museum. Roubiliac opened a studio in St Martin's Lane, and it became the meeting room of the St Martin's Lane Academy, a forerunner of the Royal Academy.

Dominique Barrière came from Marseilles and spent most of his career in Rome. There he engraved a considerable number of plates after Claude and other landscape painters. They are neatly etched in the manner of Stefano della Bella. He signed some plates Dominicus Barriere Massiliensis and others with a cipher that Domenico del Barbiere also used, so the two are often mixed up. Their styles are very different. His works include seven views of the Villa Aldobrandini from 1649.

People called Jacques Fouquier the Flemish Titian. He signed a drawing in 1604 with a note that he made it at the age of 13, which shows he was born around 1590 and not earlier, as once believed. Parish records in Antwerp show he was baptized Jacob there in December 1590. He joined the Antwerp Guild of St. Luke in 1614. Very few of his paintings survive, but engravers copied his work widely. He often worked as a painter to the court, including that of the French kings.

A painter of the Southern Netherlands, Johannes Popels belonged to the Antwerp Guild of Saint Luke from 1622 until 1663. He engraved religious subjects, and the Albertina in Vienna owns his Group of Three Naked Children. He also made copies of Italian paintings and modelli for the catalogue of the gallery of Archduke Leopold Wilhelm of Austria. David Teniers the Younger worked with him on that job. He died in Tournai.

Daguerre worked as a theatre designer before he turned to photography. He apprenticed with Pierre Prévost, the first French panorama painter, and later invented the diorama, which opened in Paris in 1822. He then partnered with Nicéphore Niépce. Niépce died in 1833, but Daguerre kept experimenting and developed the daguerreotype. The French government bought his rights in exchange for lifetime pensions for him and Niépce's son Isidore. In 1839 it presented the invention to the world as a gift.

Leloir came from a family of artists. His parents were a painter and the fashion illustrator Héloïse Colin, and his grandfather Alexandre-Marie Colin was a painter too. He tried several times for the Prix de Rome and took the Second Grand Prize in 1861. From 1868 he turned to genre scenes, drawing on medieval everyday life, Dutch-style interiors and Orientalist subjects. He illustrated books by Molière and other authors. He was made a Chevalier of the Legion of Honor in 1876.

Georg Saal painted Greenland scenes, but he probably never went there. His friend Hans Gude got him interested in Norway, and he spent several months traveling there. The pictures he brought back impressed Wilhelm von Schadow, who took him into his Master Class. Saal later became court painter in Baden-Baden and kept a second home in Paris, where he got involved with the Barbizon school. He died in 1870 of a second stroke, soon after rushing home at the start of the Siege of Paris.

Pillement turned down the chance to become court painter to King Joseph of Portugal, because he wanted to keep traveling. He was born and died in Lyon, but he worked in Paris, Madrid, Lisbon, London, Vienna and Warsaw. David Garrick and his wife became keen collectors of his work in England. In Warsaw he decorated the Royal Castle for King Stanisław II Augustus. He later worked for Marie Antoinette. His designs were engraved by printmakers, among them Anne Allen, who became his wife.

Macrino d'Alba's birth name was Gian Giacomo de' Alladio. The nickname Macrino probably came from his slim and gaunt build. Nothing is known about his early training. He is believed to have been in Rome around 1490, and his work shows an affinity with Pinturicchio's. He painted the Resurrection for the Certosa di Pavia and worked in the cathedral of Vigevano. An altarpiece of the Virgin Enthroned, dated 1503, is in the sanctuary at Crea near Casale Monferrato.

Siegwald Dahl was one of nine children of the Norwegian painter Johan Christian Dahl, and only he and one sister lived to adulthood. His father gave him his first art lessons. After three years at the Dresden Academy he went to London to study with Edwin Landseer, another famous animal painter. He spent some time in Paris too. His best known works use Norwegian motifs, inspired by his father's pictures and his many visits to Norway.

Casado del Alisal's painting The Resurrection of Lazarus won him a fellowship to study in Rome in 1855. He had begun at the municipal drawing school in Palencia and went on to the academy in Madrid under Federico de Madrazo. He also stayed in Naples, Milan and Venice. His fellowship was extended in 1861 so he could study in Paris, where he showed The Oath of the Cortes of Cádiz. That painting now hangs in the Congress of Deputies. In 1881 he became the first director of the Spanish Academy in Rome.

Károly Ferenczy went to Munich in the late nineteenth century and took free classes with the Hungarian painter Simon Hollósy. When he returned to Hungary he helped found the Nagybánya artists' colony in 1896. He became one of its major figures. The Hungarian National Gallery holds 51 of his paintings, and a museum named for him stands in his birthplace, Szentendre. He is often called the father of Hungarian impressionism.

Unkoku Tōgan was the second son of Hara Naoie, lord of Nokomi Castle in Hizen province. He started as an artist of the Kanō school, but soon took his inspiration from Sesshū. He mostly painted realistic landscapes in ink on paper. He worked under Lord Mori of Yamaguchi. Later he became a Buddhist priest and abbot of Unkoku-an Temple. He died in Yamaguchi.

Govardhan was the son of Bhavani Das, a minor painter in the imperial workshop, and like many Mughal painters they were Hindus. He joined the imperial service under Akbar and kept working until the reign of Shah Jahan. He helped illustrate the Baburnama now in the British Museum. His portraits in the Jahangir albums are in American and European museums. He showed the different human physiques of Indians with great accuracy. A contemporary, Daulat, painted a portrait of him.

Pierre Andrieu joined Delacroix's studio in 1843 and became his most trusted assistant. He worked on murals at the church of Saint-Sulpice and on decorations at the Paris City Hall. When Delacroix's huge dome painting at the Luxembourg Palace library came unglued and crashed to the ground in 1868, Andrieu renovated it. After Delacroix died in 1863 he opened his own studio. A flood ruined his home and caused money trouble, which may have led to the claim that he passed off some of his own paintings as Delacroix's. He is mainly known for copies of Delacroix.

Hermann Kauffmann the Elder painted winter scenes, such as a mail coach in a snowstorm, a sleigh track on the Elbe and fishermen on the ice. He was born in Hamburg, the son of a merchant, and studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich under Peter Heß. Back in Hamburg in 1833, he kept painting under the influence of the Bavarian landscape. He also made studies in northern and southern Germany and in Norway. His painting of the Great Fire of Hamburg hangs in the town hall. His son Hugo was a painter too.
